record_verbatim.evidence: ROOT CAUSE, read from the CMock generator source rather than inferred. 'uint64_t' appears NOWHERE in CMock 2.7.2's standard_treat_as_map (ceedling-1.1.9/vendor/cmock/lib/cmock_config.rb:141-183), which maps uint8/uint16/uint32 and their _t spellings plus the other C scalar spellings, but contains no 64-bit unsigned entry - verified by a direct search returning zero matches. It is also absent from the shipped project's own ':treat_as:' list at conf/unit/app_project_posix.yml:362-367, which lists only uint8, uint16, uint32, int8 and bool. With neither source supplying it and ':memcmp_if_unknown: true' set at conf/unit/app_project_posix.yml:368, cmock_unityhelper_parser.rb:34 does not raise and instead falls through to line 36, returning the memory fallback. For a BY-VALUE argument that yields UNITY_TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_MEMORY with the '&' argument modifier, i.e. CMock emits, for the by-value uint64_t parameter 'canSignal' of CAN_TxSetMessageDataWithSignalData (src/app/driver/can/cbs/can_helper.h:131-136): UNITY_TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_MEMORY(&cmock_call_instance->Expected_canSignal, &canSignal, sizeof(uint64_t), ...). That is an 8-byte memcmp of the ADDRESS of a scalar, so it compares two stack addresses and fails whenever the value happens to differ. Confirmed verbatim in the generated mock Mockcan_helper.c:500 and :528. Symptom before the fix, identical in both affected tests: 'Memory Mismatch. Byte 0 Expected 0x00 Was 0x38:Function CAN_TxSetMessageDataWithSignalData Argument canSignal' at test_can_cbs_tx_f_debug-build-configuration.c:698 and :1757, and 'Memory Mismatch. Byte 0 Expected 0x00 Was 0x6A' at test_can_cbs_tx_f_pack-minimum-maximum-values.c:718 and :881. Note this is a configuration defect and NOT a product defect and NOT a driver bug: can_helper.h:131 correctly declares a by-value uint64_t. FIX APPLIED, in the SIL harness configuration only (docs/artifacts/.work/verification-env/sil/run.sh, which rewrites its own isolated copy of the Ceedling project file): ':treat_as:' gains 'uint64_t: UINT64' and 'uint64: UINT64'. CMock then emits UNITY_TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_UINT64 and the assertion checks the VALUE, which is what the test means. A SECOND, GENUINE TEST DEFECT WAS EXPOSED BY THE FIX, and this is the substantive reason the finding matters. Once the assertion compared values instead of addresses, it failed with a real value mismatch: 'Expected 0 Was 18446744073709551416'. That second operand is 18446744073709551416 - 2^64 = -200, which is BC_TEMPERATURE_MIN_CHARGE_MSL_ddegC (src/app/application/config/battery_cell_cfg.h:124). The product passes '(int64_t)signalData' (can_cbs_tx_f_debug-build-configuration.c:874), the correct sign-extended conversion. The test passed 'temperatureMinChargeSignals[0u]', a float_t, directly into a uint64_t parameter. Measured on this host: (uint64_t)(-200.0f) is 0, while (uint64_t)(int64_t)(-200.0f) is 18446744073709551416. Converting a negative float to an unsigned type is not the same value as sign-extending it, so the test's EXPECTATION was 0 and the code under test was right. Under the broken address comparison this defect was invisible, because the comparison never looked at the value. The same shape appears in test_can_cbs_tx_f_pack-minimum-maximum-values.c, where testMinimumTemperature0 is -150.0f (line 99) and the product uses '(int64_t)signalData' (can_cbs_tx_f_pack-minimum-maximum-values.c:447). FIXED test-side by casting the signal fixtures through (int64_t) at the expectation sites, exactly as the product does: 81 sites in test_can_cbs_tx_f_debug-build-configuration.c and 4 in test_can_cbs_tx_f_pack-minimum-maximum-values.c, each carrying a comment recording why. The cast is confined to the test's own expectation arguments and changes no product behaviour. RESULT: test_can_cbs_tx_f_debug-build-configuration.c 23/23 and test_can_cbs_tx_f_pack-minimum-maximum-values.c 14/14, both previously 21/23 and 12/14.
record_verbatim.impact: Two distinct things were wrong and only one of them was visible before. The configuration defect made four assertions compare stack addresses, which is an assertion that cannot detect a wrong value and can fail for reasons unrelated to the code - the worst kind of oracle, because it looks like coverage. Fixing it revealed a real test defect that had been hidden underneath it for as long as the configuration had been wrong: the tests encoded an expectation of 0 where the driver correctly encodes -200, because a negative float_t was implicitly converted to uint64_t instead of sign-extended. That defect is a silent under-test of a CAN signal path, and it is exactly the kind that an address comparison cannot find. The cost of the fix is bounded and was measured: the SIL harness configuration changed, no file under src/ changed, and the two affected tests went from 21/23 and 12/14 to 23/23 and 14/14 with zero regressions across the 313-test suite. The limit must be stated: the defect in conf/unit/app_project_posix.yml is NOT fixed there. Only the SIL harness's isolated copy carries the ':treat_as:' entry. A run against the shipped conf/ on Linux or Windows will still exhibit the address-comparison behaviour and will still hide the negative-float defect. That is a product-owner decision about the shipped configuration and it is recorded here as open, not closed. Passing these two tests under the SIL harness says nothing about CAN bit packing on a real bus, about signal scaling or offset, or about any other device behaviour; the harness mocks the HAL and verifies driver logic against upstream's own assertions only. No MISRA conformance, tool-qualification or certification claim is made or implied.

record_verbatim.resolution:
RESOLVED for the condition this record asserts: uint64_t is no longer absent from the project's :treat_as: map.

WHAT FIXED IT. One line added to UPSTREAM-SHARED configuration, conf/unit/app_project_posix.yml, in the :treat_as: block, in the file's existing style and position:
    :treat_as:
      uint64_t: UINT64
      uint8: HEX8
      ...
This is a change to the configuration every foxBMS developer builds against, and it is intended to be: the gap is genuine and platform-independent, so leaving it would leave every developer on the defective comparator. The fix is deliberately minimal - one entry, no reordering, no change to :memcmp_if_unknown:, and the bare `uint64` spelling deliberately NOT added because the repository uses uint64_t throughout its own code.

EVIDENCE, RE-DERIVED 2026-09-30 FROM THE LIVE TREE. For the by-value uint64_t parameter `canSignal` of CAN_TxSetMessageDataWithSignalData (src/app/driver/can/cbs/can_helper.h:131-136), the generated mock now emits:
    UNITY_TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_UINT64(cmock_call_instance->Expected_canSignal, canSignal, ...)
where before the change it emitted:
    UNITY_TEST_ASSERT_EQUAL_MEMORY(&cmock_call_instance->Expected_canSignal, &canSignal, sizeof(uint64_t), ...)

The load-bearing fact behind the fix is unchanged and was re-confirmed by reading the generator: ceedling-1.1.9/vendor/cmock/lib/cmock_config.rb:141-183 `standard_treat_as_map` contains no 64-bit entry of any kind - no uint64, no uint64_t, no int64_t - so without a project-supplied mapping the type is genuinely unmapped and :memcmp_if_unknown: genuinely selects the memory fallback.

THIS RECORD'S OWN HARM CLAIM IS CORRECTED, and the correction matters more than the fix. Revision 2 and revision 1 described the pre-fix assertion as 'comparing two stack addresses', 'an assertion that cannot detect a wrong value', and 'the worst kind of oracle, because it looks like coverage'. Measurement contradicts all of that. The memory comparison took the address of the mock's own by-value parameter `canSignal` - a real, correctly-sized 8-byte uint64_t object - and the address of the stored expected value, so it was a byte comparison of the two values, not of their addresses. Three measurements, each against a byte-identical copy of tests/unit/app/driver/can/cbs/tx-async/test_can_cbs_tx_f_debug-build-configuration.c:
  (a) with the expected canSignal deliberately changed 0x26 -> 0x27, the PRE-fix configuration       still failed the case: 'Memory Mismatch. Byte 0 Expected 0x27 Was 0x26'. The wrong value was       detected.
  (b) the UNPERTURBED upstream test, whose (int64_t) expectations carry full 64-bit two's-complement       patterns, passed 23/23 in BOTH the pre-fix and post-fix configurations. The pre-fix oracle was       not producing false failures on the large values either.
  (c) the only real difference is the comparator chosen and the quality of the diagnostic:       'Expected 39 Was 38' (a numeric comparison) versus 'Memory Mismatch. Byte 0 Expected 0x27       Was 0x26' (a byte comparison).
So the fix is correct and worth making - it makes the configuration complete for the only 64-bit type the product uses, and it buys a typed numeric comparison and a readable diagnostic instead of a byte compare - but it did NOT rescue a blind oracle, and the earlier rounds' framing of the impact was wrong. The genuine defect the earlier rounds actually found and fixed was the SEPARATE test-side one: a negative float_t passed straight into a uint64_t parameter, which the product sign-extends. That was the real cause of the four original failures, not the comparator.

A MEASUREMENT CAVEAT WORTH RECORDING. The SIL harness structurally MASKS this defect and could not be used to demonstrate it: sil/run.sh unconditionally strips and re-inserts `uint64_t: UINT64` and `uint64: UINT64` into its own copy of project.yml on every invocation, so removing the entry from the shipped config changes nothing observable through the harness. The demonstration above required removing the mapping from the BUILD TREE's project.yml and invoking Ceedling directly, which is the state a developer running the shipped config on Linux or Windows is in. A future reader who tries to reproduce this through run.sh will get a false negative.

RESIDUAL, ENUMERATED, AND IT IS A SEPARATE DEFECT. The same gap is still present in the other three shipped unit-test configurations - conf/unit/app_project_posix.yml was the only one this authorisation named, and the other three were therefore not touched:
  conf/unit/bootloader_project_posix.yml   no uint64_t entry
  conf/unit/app_project_win32.yml          no uint64_t entry
  conf/unit/bootloader_project_win32.yml   no uint64_t entry
This is not hypothetical for the bootloader: src/bootloader/driver/can/can_bootloader-version-info.h:85 declares TEST_CANTX_TransmitBootMagic(uint64_t messageData), a by-value uint64_t parameter, so the bootloader variant mocks a by-value 64-bit argument under a configuration that does not map the type. It belongs to its own record, raised by whoever owns the remaining three configs; it is not a remainder of this one, and stating it here rather than closing over it is deliberate.

SCOPE OF THE RESULT. This is a test-configuration change and establishes nothing about foxBMS 2 product behaviour: no file under src/ changed, no register map, timing, clocking, interrupt, DMA, bus or electrical behaviour was exercised, and no CAN bit packing on a real bus was verified. The harness mocks the HAL. human_approval_status remains pending, production_authorized remains false and product_verification_credit remains false. No human approved this revision, no tool is claimed to be qualified, and no certification, ISO 26262 conformity or ASPICE capability level is claimed or implied.

record_verbatim.root_cause: Two independent defects stacked on the same four assertions. FIRST, a CMock configuration gap: uint64_t is in neither CMock's standard ':treat_as:' map nor the project's ':treat_as:' list, and ':memcmp_if_unknown: true' then converts 'CMock does not know this type' into 'compare the bytes of the argument', which for a by-value scalar means comparing the bytes of its address. CMock's generator cannot distinguish 'a pointer I was asked to dereference' from 'a scalar of a type I have no comparator for' at that point, and for the latter the address is the only thing it has. SECOND, and previously masked by the first, a test defect: the tests pass a negative float_t signal fixture directly into a uint64_t parameter, producing an expectation of 0, whereas the product sign-extends via an explicit (int64_t) cast and produces the correct two's-complement value. The first defect hid the second because the address comparison never inspected the value at all. The fix for the first is a ':treat_as:' mapping for uint64_t; that alone is not sufficient to make the tests pass, and treating it as sufficient would have left four assertions failing for a reason that has nothing to do with the configuration.
